question: What is the minimum recommended length for a strong password?
options: 8 characters
10 characters
12 characters
16 characters
explanation: While 8 characters was once standard, modern computing power makes 12+ characters the recommended minimum for strong passwords.

question: Which of these passwords would have the highest entropy?
options: P@ssw0rd123!
correct-horse-battery-staple
X7#mK9$pL2
Tr0ub4dor&3
explanation: Passphrases like 'correct-horse-battery-staple' (4 random words) have high entropy because of their length (25+ chars) while remaining memorable.

question: What does MFA stand for and why is it important?
options: Multi-Factor Authentication - adds a second verification step beyond passwords
Master File Access - controls who can access system files
Memory Forensics Analysis - analyzes RAM for threats
Managed Firewall Appliance - hardware firewall device
explanation: MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) requires two or more independent categories of credentials: something you know (password), something you have (phone/authenticator), or something you are (biometric).

question: Why should you use a unique password for every account?
options: It's required by law in most countries
If one service is breached, your other accounts stay secure
Password managers only work with unique passwords
It makes passwords easier to remember
explanation: Credential stuffing attacks use username/password pairs from one breach to try logging into other services. Unique passwords prevent a single breach from compromising multiple accounts.

question: You receive an email from 'security@paypal-services.com' saying your account is locked. The link goes to 'paypal-login.verification-services.xyz'. What should you do?
options: Click the link and log in to secure your account
Reply to the email asking for verification
Report as phishing and visit paypal.com directly
Forward to friends to warn them
explanation: This is a classic phishing attempt. Legitimate companies use their own domains (paypal.com), not subdomains on unrelated domains.

question: Which is a common sign of a phishing email?
options: Generic greeting, urgent language, suspicious link
Personalised greeting, calm tone, safe link
Official sender address, no attachments
All of the above
explanation: Phishing often uses generic greetings, urgency, and links that don't match the claimed sender.

question: You get an SMS: 'Your UPI payment of ₹5,000 is pending. Reply YES to confirm or call 1800-123-4567.' What should you do?
options: Reply YES
Ignore & block the number
Call the number provided
Reply with your bank details
explanation: Legitimate services never ask you to reply YES via SMS to confirm a payment. This is smishing.

question: What is 'quishing'?
options: Phishing via QR codes
Phishing via voice calls
Phishing via social media
Phishing via USB drives
explanation: Quishing = QR code phishing. Attackers place malicious QR codes in public places that lead to phishing sites when scanned.

question: What is the primary difference between a virus and a worm?
options: Viruses are more destructive than worms
Worms require user interaction to spread; viruses spread automatically
Viruses require a host file to attach to; worms are standalone and self-replicating
There is no difference - they are the same thing
explanation: Viruses attach to legitimate files/programs and require user execution to spread. Worms are standalone programs that self-replicate and spread automatically.

question: Ransomware typically spreads through which vectors? (Most common)
options: Infected USB drives left in parking lots
Phishing emails with malicious attachments/links and exploit kits
Bluetooth connections in public places
QR codes on restaurant menus
explanation: The vast majority of ransomware infections start with phishing emails containing malicious attachments or links to exploit kits.

question: What should you do immediately if you suspect ransomware?
options: Pay the ransom quickly to get your files back
Disconnect from network/internet, don't power off, contact IT/security
Run a full antivirus scan immediately
Try to decrypt files using online tools
explanation: Disconnecting prevents spread to network shares. Don't power off (may lose encryption keys in memory). Never pay ransom.

question: What is a 'botnet'?
options: A network of robots controlled by AI
A network of compromised computers controlled by an attacker
A type of antivirus software
A blockchain network
explanation: A botnet is a collection of malware-infected devices (bots) controlled remotely by an attacker (botmaster).

question: What does 'end-to-end encryption' mean?
options: Data is encrypted on your device and only decrypted on the recipient's device
Data is encrypted while traveling but decrypted on company servers
Data is encrypted with two different keys
Data is encrypted at the end of each day
explanation: E2EE means only the communicating users can read messages. The service provider cannot access the content.

question: Which is NOT a good privacy practice?
options: Using a privacy-focused browser with tracker blocking
Granting all app permissions 'just in case'
Reviewing privacy settings on social media regularly
Using a VPN on public Wi-Fi
explanation: Granting unnecessary permissions exposes your data. Follow the principle of least privilege.

question: What is 'data minimization'?
options: Compressing data to save storage space
Collecting only the data strictly necessary for a specific purpose
Deleting data after 30 days automatically
Encrypting data to minimize exposure
explanation: Data minimization is a core privacy principle: only collect, process, and retain the minimum personal data needed.

question: Biggest risk of installing apps from unknown sources (sideloading)?
options: Apps won't update automatically
Apps may contain malware since they bypass app store review
Apps will drain battery faster
Apps won't work on newer Android versions
explanation: Official app stores review apps for malware. Sideloaded apps bypass this protection.

question: What is SIM swapping?
options: Switching SIM cards between phones
Attacker convinces carrier to transfer your number to their SIM
A malware that clones your SIM card remotely
A feature that lets you use two numbers on one SIM
explanation: SIM swapping is when attackers social-engineer carriers to port your phone number to their SIM, intercepting 2FA codes.

question: Most secure screen lock method?
options: Pattern lock
4-digit PIN
6-digit PIN or alphanumeric password
Face unlock (basic)
explanation: 6-digit PIN has 1,000,000 combinations vs 10,000 for 4-digit. Alphanumeric passwords are even stronger.

question: What is 'credential stuffing'?
options: Stuffing multiple credentials into a login form at once
Using stolen username/password pairs from one breach to try other sites
Hiding credentials in website code
A password manager feature
explanation: Credential stuffing automates login attempts using credentials from data breaches.

question: You get a call from 'Microsoft Support' saying your computer has a virus. They ask for remote access. What do you do?
options: Grant access - Microsoft does proactively monitor computers
Ask for their employee ID and call back on the official number
Hang up - Microsoft never makes unsolicited support calls
Pay the fee they request to fix the 'virus'
explanation: This is a tech support scam. Microsoft never makes unsolicited calls about computer viruses.

question: What is a 'zero-day' vulnerability?
options: A vulnerability known for zero days
A vulnerability unknown to the vendor with no patch available
A vulnerability that affects zero users
A vulnerability that requires zero clicks to exploit
explanation: A zero-day vulnerability is unknown to the vendor, meaning no patch exists.

question: What does a VPN actually protect?
options: Your data from your ISP and network eavesdroppers on public Wi-Fi
You from all viruses and malware
Your identity from websites you visit
Your passwords from keyloggers
explanation: A VPN encrypts traffic between your device and the VPN server, protecting from ISP and eavesdroppers.

question: How can you best protect against SIM swapping?
options: Don't share your phone number online
Set up a PIN/password with your mobile carrier for account changes
Use SMS-based 2FA everywhere
Turn off your phone at night
explanation: Contact your carrier to set up a port-out PIN. This prevents attackers from social-engineering carrier support.

question: What is the purpose of a 'salt' in password hashing?
options: To make passwords taste better
To add random data to each password before hashing, preventing rainbow table attacks
To encrypt the password database
To slow down the hashing process
explanation: A salt is unique random data added to each password before hashing, ensuring identical passwords produce different hashes.

question: Spot the scam: You receive an email - "Subject: Your Netflix account is suspended. Click here to reactivate: netflix-secure-login.xyz/confirm". Is this a phishing attempt?
options: Legitimate Netflix email
Phishing scam
A legitimate Netflix renewal notice
A harmless marketing newsletter
explanation: The sender address is not @netflix.com and the link goes to a suspicious domain (xyz instead of com).

question: Spot the scam: An SMS reads - "Your UPI payment of ₹5,000 is pending. Reply YES to confirm or call 1800-123-4567." What should you do?
options: Reply YES
Ignore & block the number
Call the number
Reply STOP to opt out
explanation: Legitimate services never ask you to reply YES via SMS to confirm a payment. This is smishing.

question: Spot the scam: A QR code on a "Free Wi-Fi" flyer at a café opens http://free-wifi-guest.tk when scanned. Is the QR code safe?
options: Safe - gives free Wi-Fi
Scam - leads to a phishing site
Safe if the cafe looks reputable
Safe if the QR code is printed on official paper
explanation: Unverified QR codes can direct you to malicious sites that steal credentials or install malware.

question: Spot the scam: You get an email - "Subject: IT Department: Password Expiry Notice" with an attachment named password-reset-form.pdf. Is this legitimate?
options: Legitimate IT notice
Phishing scam
A routine HR policy update
A legitimate security awareness test
explanation: Unexpected password expiry notices with attachments are classic phishing. IT departments typically email, not attach PDFs.

question: Spot the scam: An SMS reads - "You won ₹1,00,000! Click here to claim: bit.ly/freemoney". What type of scam is this?
options: Lottery scam
Legitimate prize
A bank reward notification
A tax refund notification
explanation: You can't win a lottery you didn't enter. This is a classic advance-fee fraud scheme.

question: Spot the scam: Is this URL safe - https://paypall-security-update.com/verify-account ?
options: Safe - PayPal security page
Fake - lookalike domain
Safe because the page uses HTTPS
A PayPal regional partner site
explanation: The domain has "paypall" (double L) instead of "paypal". This is a typo-squatting phishing site.

question: Spot the scam: Your CEO emails - "Urgent: Wire Transfer Request. Transfer $50,000 to this vendor immediately." Is this a business email compromise risk?
options: Legitimate CEO request
Business email compromise
A routine vendor payment request
An internal audit request
explanation: Even from a familiar sender, verify wire transfer requests through a separate channel (phone call).

question: Spot the scam: An SMS reads - "Your package is held at customs. Pay ₹2,000 release fee: http://customs-verify.tk". What is this?
options: Legitimate customs notice
Smishing scam
A courier tracking update
A government customs notice
explanation: Customs agencies don't send payment links via SMS for released packages. This is a delivery scam.

question: Spot the scam: Identify the threat - http://irda-login-security-update.in/verify
options: Legitimate insurance portal
Phishing site
The official IRDAI website
A bank insurance partner page
explanation: The .in domain claiming to be IRDAI (Insurance Regulatory Authority) is a phishing site mimicking a legitimate authority.

question: Spot the scam: An email says - "We want to hire you! Transfer setup kit money via Zelle, we'll reimburse." Is this a job scam?
options: Legitimate job offer
Job scam
A legitimate staffing agency offer
A paid internship with a placement fee
explanation: Legitimate employers never ask new employees to transfer money or use personal payment apps.

question: Which device usually acts as the first line of defence between your home network and the internet?
options: The router (with its built-in firewall)
The printer
A smart speaker
The monitor
explanation: The router sits between your devices and the internet, so its firewall and firmware are your first line of defence.

question: What does HTTPS actually guarantee?
options: That traffic between your browser and the site is encrypted
That the site owner is honest
That the site contains no malware
That your identity is verified to the site
explanation: HTTPS encrypts the connection; it says nothing about whether the site is trustworthy.

question: What is the main risk of signing into accounts over an open public Wi-Fi network without a VPN?
options: Other devices on that network may intercept your unencrypted traffic
Your laptop battery drains faster
Your browser loses its saved bookmarks
The Wi-Fi owner can read your local files directly
explanation: On shared or rogue networks an attacker can capture traffic; a VPN or mobile data removes that exposure.

question: A VPN mainly hides your traffic from which party?
options: The local network and your internet provider
The website you are visiting
Your operating system
The website certificate authority
explanation: A VPN tunnels traffic past the local network and ISP; the destination site still sees your requests.

question: Which change makes a home router meaningfully safer?
options: Changing the default admin password and disabling WPS
Renaming the Wi-Fi to something official
Hiding the SSID only
Using the same password as your email
explanation: Default admin credentials and WPS are common entry points; changing them and updating firmware matters far more than hiding the SSID.

question: What is network segmentation?
options: Splitting a network into isolated zones so a breach cannot spread freely
Splitting large files into packets
Using several Wi-Fi extenders
Encrypting every packet twice
explanation: Segmentation limits lateral movement: an infected guest or IoT device cannot reach servers holding sensitive data.

question: What does DNSSEC protect against?
options: Forged DNS answers that redirect you to the wrong server
Weak Wi-Fi passwords
Phishing emails that never use links
Malware inside attachments
explanation: DNSSEC cryptographically signs DNS records so a spoofed answer (cache poisoning) can be detected.

question: Which port does HTTPS use by default?
explanation: HTTPS defaults to TCP 443, while plain HTTP uses port 80.

question: What is ARP spoofing typically used for on a local network?
options: Positioning the attacker as a man-in-the-middle
Cracking Wi-Fi encryption
Speeding up local file transfers
Blocking spam emails
explanation: Fake ARP replies make your device send traffic to the attacker, who can then read or alter it.

question: Why should you install router firmware updates?
options: They patch security holes attackers actively exploit
They make the Wi-Fi signal stronger
They increase your data plan
They remove the need for a password
explanation: Unpatched routers are a favourite target for botnets; firmware updates close known flaws.

question: Which combination is most dangerous to post publicly?
options: Full name, date of birth and an ID or account number
Your favourite colour
A photo of your pet
Your favourite movie
explanation: That combination is exactly what many identity checks ask for, so it enables impersonation.

question: Which is a classic early signal of identity theft?
options: A loan application or credit account you never opened
A newsletter you subscribed to
A delivery arriving early
A password reset you requested yourself
explanation: Accounts opened in your name show up on your credit report long before the debt collectors call.

question: How can you check whether someone opened accounts in your name?
options: Review your credit report regularly for unknown accounts
Search your name on social media
Check your Wi-Fi signal strength
Change your email signature
explanation: A credit report lists credit accounts and enquiries, making it the standard check for identity fraud.

question: What does account takeover usually rely on first?
options: Reused or stolen credentials combined with weak recovery options
Physical theft of your laptop
A slow internet connection
Too many browser tabs
explanation: Attackers rarely "hack" the account: they reuse leaked passwords or abuse recovery channels.

question: Your Aadhaar number has been exposed. What is the most useful first step?
options: Monitor accounts, lock your credit where possible and report misuse
Delete your email account
Change your phone number immediately
Ignore it, Aadhaar numbers are public
explanation: You cannot change the number, but you can watch for misuse, add alerts and report fraud quickly.

question: Why is reusing your email password especially risky for identity theft?
options: Email controls password resets for almost every other account
Email passwords are stored in plain text
Email companies sell passwords
Email is always unencrypted
explanation: Whoever controls your email can reset your bank, social and shopping accounts.

question: What is synthetic identity fraud?
options: Combining real and fake details to create a new identity that passes checks
Using someone else's photo online
Creating an AI-generated profile picture
Stealing a physical ID card
explanation: Fraudsters mix a real identifier (often a child's or unused SSN/PAN) with invented details to build credit.

question: A ransomware screen demands payment to unlock your files. What should you do first?
options: Disconnect from the network and restore from a clean backup
Pay quickly to get a discount
Restart the computer repeatedly
Email the attackers your ID proof
explanation: Paying funds crime without guaranteeing recovery; isolating the machine and restoring a backup is the safe path.

question: How does fileless malware usually avoid antivirus detection?
options: It runs in memory using trusted system tools instead of dropping a file
It hides in your photos
It only runs when the PC is off
It encrypts itself with your Wi-Fi password
explanation: Living in memory and abusing PowerShell or WMI leaves few artefacts on disk for scanners to find.

question: What does "living off the land" mean in an intrusion?
options: Using legitimate built-in tools to avoid raising alarms
Hiding malware in a farm app
Attacking only offline computers
Stealing physical hard drives
explanation: Attackers use signed utilities like PowerShell, PsExec or WMI so their activity blends into normal admin work.

question: Why are offline or immutable backups critical against ransomware?
options: Ransomware cannot encrypt backups it cannot reach
They make the computer faster
They replace the need for antivirus
They automatically decrypt files
explanation: Connected drives and network shares get encrypted too; an offline copy is what makes recovery possible.

question: What is double-extortion ransomware?
options: Encrypting files and also threatening to publish stolen data
Encrypting the same file twice
Demanding payment in two currencies
Infecting two computers at once
explanation: Data is exfiltrated before encryption, so paying for the key does not stop a leak threat.

question: What is a deepfake?
options: AI-generated audio or video that convincingly imitates a real person
A photo with a deep shadow
A fake Wi-Fi hotspot
An email with a spoofed sender name
explanation: Deepfakes synthesise faces or voices, and are used for fraud, blackmail and disinformation.

question: What is a prompt injection attack against an AI assistant?
options: Hidden instructions in content that hijack the assistant's behaviour
Flooding the assistant with too many questions
Guessing the assistant's password
Injecting malware into the AI model file
explanation: Text inside a web page or document can contain instructions the model follows, overriding its intended task.

question: How is AI voice cloning most often used by scammers?
options: To impersonate a relative or executive and demand urgent money
To improve call-centre accents
To translate videos
To generate stronger passwords
explanation: A few seconds of public audio is enough to fake a distressed relative asking for an urgent transfer.

question: What makes LLM-written phishing emails more dangerous than older templates?
options: They are fluent, context-aware and free of the grammar tells people were taught to spot
They bypass HTTPS
They cannot be filtered at all
They always come from a real bank domain
explanation: Polished, personalised language removes the classic "bad grammar" warning sign, so verify senders instead.

question: What is a zero-click exploit?
options: An attack that works without the victim clicking or opening anything
A phishing link with no destination
An email with an empty body
An ad that costs nothing
explanation: Zero-click attacks abuse flaws in messaging or media handling, so patching is the main defence.

question: Why should you avoid pasting personal or work data into public AI chatbots?
options: The data may be stored, logged or reused by the provider
The chatbot will answer more slowly
It uses more battery
It breaks the chat window
explanation: Anything you paste can leave your control, so treat chatbots as public and never share secrets or personal records.

question: What is phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS)?
options: Criminal kits and subscriptions that let non-experts run phishing campaigns
A legitimate email marketing platform
A government anti-phishing programme
A browser setting that blocks spam
explanation: PhaaS sells ready-made fake pages, hosting and campaign tools, which is why phishing quality has risen sharply.

question: Why is an authenticator app generally safer than SMS for one-time codes?
options: SMS codes can be intercepted or stolen through SIM swapping
SMS codes expire instantly
Authenticator codes never expire
Apps do not need a password
explanation: SMS depends on the mobile network and your SIM; app codes are generated locally and are not readable by a SIM swap.

question: Why are passkeys considered phishing-resistant?
options: They are bound to the website's origin, so a lookalike site cannot use them
They are longer than passwords
They are stored in your browser history
They change every 30 seconds
explanation: Passkeys use public-key cryptography tied to the real domain, so a fake login page gets nothing reusable.

question: How does spear phishing differ from bulk phishing?
options: It is researched and personalised for one person or team
It only targets mobile phones
It never contains links
It is always sent by SMS
explanation: Spear phishing uses real names, projects and relationships, which makes the request far more convincing.

question: A supplier emails new bank details for an unpaid invoice. What is the safest response?
options: Call the supplier on a number you already have and verify before paying
Reply asking them to confirm by email
Pay quickly to avoid late fees
Forward it to a colleague to check later
explanation: Invoice and bank-detail changes are the core of business email compromise; verify out-of-band with a known number.

question: What is MFA fatigue (push bombing)?
options: Spamming approval prompts until the victim accepts one
Forgetting your second factor
Using MFA on too many sites
A slow authenticator app
explanation: Repeated push notifications, sometimes paired with a fake support call, wear the victim down into approving.

question: A buyer says you must approve a UPI "collect request" before they can pay you. What actually happens?
options: Money leaves your account instead of arriving
You receive the money instantly
Nothing happens until you scan a QR code
The bank holds the amount for 24 hours
explanation: Approving a collect request debits you; receiving money never needs a PIN or an approval.

question: What characterises a "safe account" scam?
options: A caller convinces you to move money to an account "for safekeeping"
A bank opens a savings account for you
An escrow service holds payment for a purchase
A wallet with two-factor authentication
explanation: No bank or police force asks you to transfer funds to a "safe" account; once transferred, the money is gone.

question: What is a privacy policy for?
options: Explaining what data a service collects and how it is used
Guaranteeing the service is secure
Listing the company's employees
Blocking cookies automatically
explanation: It is a disclosure of data practices, not a security guarantee.

question: What is the main purpose of India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023?
options: Giving people rights over their personal data and requiring consent
Banning all data collection
Regulating only government websites
Replacing the IT Act entirely
explanation: The DPDP Act sets consent, purpose-limitation and data-principal rights for digital personal data.

question: What does the "right to erasure" allow?
options: Asking an organisation to delete personal data it no longer needs
Deleting your browser history only
Removing your name from search results permanently
Erasing data from backups instantly
explanation: It is a data-subject right to have personal data deleted, subject to legal retention requirements.

question: What is the key difference between anonymisation and pseudonymisation?
options: Anonymised data cannot be re-linked to a person; pseudonymised data can
They are the same thing
Pseudonymisation deletes all data
Anonymisation only applies to photos
explanation: Pseudonymised records keep a mapping key, so they remain personal data under most privacy laws.

question: Why can simply removing names still fail to anonymise a dataset?
options: Combinations of remaining details can re-identify people
Names are never personal data
Anonymisation only works on paper
Removing names always satisfies the law
explanation: Age, postcode and job can uniquely identify someone; true anonymisation needs stronger techniques.

question: What does the padlock in your browser address bar prove?
options: The connection is encrypted - not that the site is trustworthy
The site has been audited for safety
The site cannot contain malware
The company is registered
explanation: Padlocks only confirm encryption; phishing sites can have valid certificates too.

question: Why should you review the permissions of a browser extension before installing it?
options: Extensions can read and change data on every site you visit
Extensions always slow the browser down
Extensions cannot be removed later
Extensions use your camera by default
explanation: A malicious or compromised extension can read pages, cookies and form data across all your tabs.

question: What is the safest way to handle a software download from an unfamiliar site?
options: Verify the publisher and scan the file before running it
Run it immediately to see if it works
Disable antivirus first
Rename the file before opening
explanation: Downloads are a top malware vector; prefer official sources and scan anything unexpected.

question: What is a homograph (IDN) attack?
options: Using lookalike Unicode characters to fake a trusted domain
Attacking a website with too many images
Sending the same email twice
Registering a domain with two hyphens
explanation: Characters from other scripts can render almost identically to Latin letters, creating convincing fake domains.
